The Karnataka High Court has directed the authorities not to proceed with the deportation of a person suspected to be an illegal immigrant from Bangladesh without first providing him a fair and reasonable opportunity to establish his claim of Indian citizenship by birth and determining his nationality through an adequate procedure in accordance with law.
Justice C.M. Poonacha, while disposing of a writ petition filed by Abdul Rahim, who was confined to the Utile Foundation (UF) at Kothanur in Bengaluru following a movement restriction order issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer (FRRO), directed the authorities to take steps expeditiously to ascertain his nationality after affording him an adequate opportunity to present his case.
The petitioner had challenged the FRRO’s March 5, 2026, order directing him to remain at the UF until his repatriation, issued on the ground that he was a Bangladeshi national and there was a likelihood of his disappearing and indulging in undesirable activities.
Mr. Rahim, however, claimed that he was an Indian citizen by birth and had been residing in India for several decades. He contended that he was born in New Seemapuri, Delhi, on April 14, 1979, and had moved to Bengaluru in 2014, where he was engaged in waste management and scrap trading through his proprietorship concern.
He relied on several documents, including a passport issued in 2018, a voter identity card issued in 2005, an Aadhaar card, a PAN card, a driving licence, and other government-issued certificates to substantiate his claim.
Opposing the petition, the authorities contended that Mr. Rahim was a Bangladeshi national who had relied on fabricated and fraudulent documents to claim Indian citizenship.
The FRRO also pointed out discrepancies in the birth certificates produced by him in two different proceedings. It submitted that the hospital where he claimed to have been born was established only in December 1995 and, therefore, could not have issued a birth record relating to 1979. The authorities also disputed the genuineness of his father’s death certificate and other documents.
The court, however, observed that the authorities ought to have considered the various documents relied upon by the petitioner and provided him with an opportunity to establish his citizenship before passing an order restricting his movement.
Though the petitioner was convicted by a court in Ghaziabad in Uttar Pradesh in 2010 under Section 14A(b) of the Foreigners Act, 1946, for illegal entry into India, Justice Poonacha noted that the Allahabad High Court later granted him bail and that all these materials were not considered by the FRRO in passing the order for his deportation.
The court clarified that possession of such documents did not, by itself, conclusively establish Indian citizenship. However, the authorities could not disregard them without undertaking an appropriate examination.
Paragraph 16 of the Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025, the court pointed out, contains a provision for referring the question of whether a person is a foreigner to a Foreigners Tribunal.
The court, however, declined to determine Mr. Rahim’s citizenship for the first time in the writ proceedings, leaving the issue to be decided by the competent authorities through the prescribed legal process.
